title: First GTA 6 Actor Officially Confirmed, And It’s A Big Name
description: There's been speculation for months over who could be voicing the GTA 6 cast, but nothing has been officially confirmed, either by developer Rockstar or any of the starring talents, until now. At the BAFTA TV Tea Party, held at The Maybourne Beverly Hills in California, actor Stephen Root was attending in support of his Emmy nomination for his role as Wyck in Apple's Widow's Bay. However, when asked about the rumors around his involvement in GTA 6, Root confirmed (via AP ) that he does appear in the game. "Yeah, you're going to see me in there," he confirmed. "I think from the first rollout of GTA that they were doing almost a year ago they had my character in there, and there were too many people that knew me from King of the Hill and my voice. So, I think that secret kind of got divulged then." "I'm so happy to be involved with it; it's an amazing thing to look at," he added. Root, who is known for voicing King of the Hill's Bill Dauterive and playing Milton Waddams in Office Space among hundreds of other credits, will play Brian Heder. Although he didn't confirm as much in the interview clip from AP, Root's distinctive voice makes him easy to pick out from the various GTA 6 trailers. Root played Office Space's Milton Waddams. Brian is a veteran drug smuggler working around the Leonida Keys area and also seems to be protagonist Jason Duval's landlord--although he doesn't charge him any rent. Rather than just a random NPC, Brian seems to be a key figure in the story of GTA 6. He's got his own profile on the official GTA 6 website, for a start. That profile notes that Brian's still moving drugs through his boatyard with his third wife, Lori, but prefers to let others do his dirty work. GTA 6 will be released on November 19 on PS5 and Xbox Series X|S, and Rockstar is hard at work fighting drones and hackers to keep the game's secrets safe.

title: Wardogs Patch Notes – Scheduled Maintenance And Patch 0.11
description: Over the weekend, Wardogs hit a mammoth peak concurrent count of over 425,000. Today, the game is undergoing scheduled maintenance to improve the server browser experience for players. The servers will be down on Monday, 14 September from 1 AM PT / 4 AM ET / 9 AM GMT for approximately one hour while the patch is deployed. Here's everything included in that patch and what it means for your Wardogs experience. Server Browser Improvements In the patch notes, Wardogs developer Bulkhead acknowledges that the server browsing experience hasn't been as good as it should be. "Community servers have been underserved, and the server browser experience as a whole has been poor," the developer writes. "It is clear to us that we have not put the same amount of care and passion into community servers that we have into the rest of the game." As a result, Bulkhead says it "worked through the night" to put together an update that will "start the process" of improving the server browser, with a focus on community servers. "Community servers are the lifeblood of FPS games like ours," Bulkhead adds. This means that the developer will be "actively" creating technology to support the growth of communities. "We have failed to do that by rushing our community server strategy. As we've always said, when we're wrong, we'll hold our hands up. We got this bit wrong." To address this, Bulkhead will be making the following changes to the server browser: New front-end browser split into community and official There will be a new interface appearing when searching for a server. "A game with this many players realistically should be using matchmaking, and server browsers aren't massively fit for purpose, but we don't want community admins and hosts to suffer." This option for players allows you to choose between joining official or community servers, but doesn't make the experience unfairly weighted toward official servers. title: How To Win Matches In Wardogs
description: Wardogs has been released into early access on PC. This is a large-scale tactical warfare game, where you can play various roles in order to help your team score enough points to reach a victory. In this guide, we'll explain how matches of Wardogs are played and how you can earn points for your team. Wardogs matches explained This game features matches with large teams fighting for control of a circular "Control Zone" designated on the map. The goal is to have your team hold the majority in this zone in order to score points. About every 30 seconds, the team with the most players in this Control Zone will earn one point, and the first team to 100 wins. Wardogs victory screen This sounds simple enough, but there is an additional moving "Hot Zone," which is highlighted in yellow on the map. Each player standing in the Hot Zone counts as two players toward the score, offering teams a way to quickly swing control in their favor if they can get players into this smaller zone. Controlling towers on the map can also help your team secure a path to victory, and we'll explain more about them below. Wardogs features a massive map with sandbox-style gameplay, so there are many ways you can help your team secure the zone and the win. Money system and loadouts Matches feature an in-game money system, and you'll use this cash to purchase weapons, supplies, vehicles, and equipment for each life. Yes, you lose everything when you die. This means you'll purchase a custom loadout for each life, but you'll keep your cash earned between matches. You'll begin your very first match with $10,000, but it won't take you long to start building up better funds to work with. As you level up, you'll unlock better guns, armor, vehicles, and equipment. This will become crucial to you and your team's success. title: How To Level Up Each Skill In Wardogs
description: Wardogs has officially launched in early access, and while it doesn't feature class-specific roles like Battlefield, there are several different skill branches you can level up to make yourself more efficient. In this guide, we'll explain each skill type in Wardogs and how to level each one. How skills work in Wardogs Wardogs player progression There are six skill tracks in Wardogs: Assault Medic Recon Support Driver Pilot Instead of forcing you to pick a class type at the start of your match, Wardogs lets you gain XP by completing various role-specific actions throughout each match. This means you can complete several different action types to level up multiple skills in a single match. All of the skill levels are added up to give you a player level, and this general leveling will unlock new ammo types, armor, items, and more. You don't have to commit to leveling each skill type, but there are some good items locked behind these specific skills, so it's worth knowing what actions will level you up and what you can unlock. We'll break down how to level each skill below. How to level each skill in Wardogs Assault The assault class rewards XP for getting kills and assists. Leveling up the assault class will give you access to more assault rifles and various attachments. Medic Medic track progression The medic class rewards you for reviving and healing your teammates. To get the most out of this role, make sure you're bringing a few bandages into each match, so you can get awarded with money and XP for healing teammates after you revive them. You do not get credit for reviving yourself. Playing a medic role is always helpful in team-based shooter games, and Wardogs is no exception. You can earn a lot of money by reviving and healing your teammates, and it will also reward you with plenty of XP to level up and unlock more efficient medical gear, including defibrillators and a medical bag. Even if you don't want to play a healer role, it's still worth leveling up enough…

title: You’ll Fight The Protoss In StarCraft, Too, Don’t Worry
description: StarCraft's reveal trailer squarely put the focus on the Terrans, who later in the cinematic face a terrifying confrontation with the Zerg. The franchise's three franchises--including the Protoss--have always been a central element of what distinguishes StarCraft from other strategy games. Although the Protoss were effectively absent from the trailer, they are a foe you will face at some point. GameSpot spoke with GM and creative director Dan Hay at BlizzCon and asked him about how the three factions will interact with each other. Although he was expectedly coy on specifics, he did offer up some thoughts. "The answer to that question is I absolutely unequivocally can't say," Hay said. "But what I can do is tell you what I would want as a player. I'll hint at sort of not what we're doing, but some of the things that we think about. "Of course, what you want to be able to do... you think about the Protoss and how reverent we are. They're older, and there's a mystique and a grandness to them, right? They have just a completely different flavor. Then you have the Zerg, and the Zerg are just numberless; they're infinite from the standpoint of they just overwhelm you with sheer organic power. Then you have the Terrans, that are this group of... they're working their way through the sector in kind of a haphazard and industrial way. We want that feeling. "We want it to not all just be one taste. So we want to have moments where you're fighting things that are organic, and then moments where you're fighting things that are this wonderful legacy and that are ancient. I want to tell you a lot more, but I can't." Hay did point out something that was easy to miss in the trailer: a small hint of the Protoss. "You saw more than the Zerg in the trailer," he said. "If you look a little deeper, there's a moment when the thing opens and you hear that great horn go off. title: The StarCraft Shooter Is A Third-Person Game, And Blizzard Insists That You Have To Feel “Powerful”
description: If you walked away from the StarCraft reveal excited for the franchise to return, but unsure what this new game even is, you're not alone. Aside from being described during the BlizzCon Opening Ceremony as an open-world shooter, Blizzard didn't share much else. In an interview with GameSpot, Blizzard GM Dan Hay provided a few more details, including the fact that it's a third-person game. The StarCraft franchise, having taken the form of real-time strategy games previously, has typically used an isometric perspective. When it came to choosing what perspective to offer in the new shooter, it sounds like it wasn't a difficult decision. "Oh, that's easy," Hay said when GameSpot asked him about whether StarCraft will be a first- or third-person game. "I want to be able to see my armor. First thing we did is we built it, put it on a turntable, and spun it around like, 'Ah, awesome, cool!' I want to be able to see it, so third-person, right? "That doesn't mean that we don't have the license to, in a couple of spaces, do a little bit different and whatnot, but third-person: You get to see your armor, you get to see the full weight of everything you have, and then you get to see stuff that's in my head that I can't tell you." Hay spoke to us a great deal about the fantasy of having this armor to protect you. Asked about character progression or customization, he said, "If I was to get—in theory, hypothetically, purely hypothetically—this is what I would want: I would want to be able to make sure that my armor can be made better, stronger, and different. I would also want to be able to make sure that I could make it feel like mine. I would want it to be a visitation of the legacy of the things that I had done. I would want to show that it looked different from the first moment that I got it to the last moment I got it. So, read into that how much you will hypothetically, but that's what I would want as a player." "We have to make sure that we're thinking about—and I have to…

title: StarCraft Reboot Is “Focusing On Single-Player,” Creative Director Says
description: StarCraft is "focusing on single-player," StarCraft creative director and general manager Dan Hay and associate manager of development operations Anna Lee Hertling said in an interview with GameSpot. One of the biggest announcements of BlizzCon 2026 was the return of StarCraft, described as an open-world shooter and slated for a 2030 release. Aside from its impressive reveal cinematic, there wasn't much additional information about how StarCraft would play or what the shooter reboot of the RTS franchise would entail. Now, we have some more details. When asked whether StarCraft would be single-player or co-op, Hay said the team is "focusing on single player." "We are focused right now on the conversation of focusing on single-player, focusing on that Marine fantasy, and then making sure that we think about what it is to be that character," Hay said. "That's what we're saying for now." He said players will play as a named character that can "build a reputation and a rapport" with other in-game characters. He said the game's story will have a beginning, middle, and an "end," and that Blizzard wants it to feel like a "boxed product." Thought it's story will have an end, Hay said Blizzard wants the game to be one players can visit, explore, leave, and come back to. "We like a named character, right?" Hay said. "When it comes down to this, we want to be able to make sure that what you have is a character that has a name, a character that people in the world can know. What it does it it makes the story have a little bit more life to it." Hay continued: "What you want to be able to do is have people--and I have to be super careful, Anna Lee will abosultey stop me if I talk too much about the story--but there's nothing...I think about a TV show like Deadwood, which is one of my top five favorites. What I love is the idea that all of those characters know each other and they have a reputation. You go in, and they know each other on a Tuesday; they know each other on a…

title: Blizzard Explains Why The StarCraft Shooter Coming In 2030 Was Announced Now
description: Thanks to rumors and reports, the announcement of a new StarCraft game taking the form of an open-world shooter did not come as a complete surprise at BlizzCon's Opening Ceremony. What is surprising is when it's coming: 2030. That's a long time from now, and we've heard other developers lament announcing their games too soon. So what made Blizzard reveal StarCraft so far in advance? "We totally get the question. You walk that kind of knife's edge of how much do we want to show, when do we want to show," Blizzard GM Dan Hay told GameSpot at BlizzCon. "We've been working on it for a little bit now, and we feel like we've got something that we wanted to show. We felt like this was the right moment. As we're building out the story, the characters, and kind of the feeling of the worlds that we're building, we felt like, 'You know what? We've got enough to show.'" Hay said that with Blizzard being confident in what it's developed so far, it didn't want to further delay going public and getting the benefit of putting it in front of fans. "There's a moment when you're making a game where you're like, 'Have we landed the emotion? Do we feel like we have enough of the verve, the identity, and the feel of it to start to share it?'" Hay continued. "About a year ago, we started to feel like we were there, so we were like, 'Okay, it's time to show it. It's time to get feedback.' "What's super important about it is you want to put it out there, get people to feel the emotion and the value of it, and you want to be there live to be able to get a sense of how they feel about it. We were in the room; it felt great. People were going nuts." Feedback from fans at this point can only be surface level. Although we know the new game, known at least for now simply as StarCraft, is an open-world shooter, we've yet to see any gameplay--the reveal took the form of an extended cinematic setting up the vibe, but not tipping Blizzard's hand in terms of how it will play. title: Diablo 4’s Expansion Days Are Over
description: Diablo 4 won't receive more expansions moving forward, as Blizzard shifts its focus to the newly revealed Diablo 5 instead. As revealed during BlizzCon 2026's opening ceremony, Diablo 5 is slated to be coming in Spring 2029 and is set 100 years after Diablo 4 in a world where the titular Lord of Terror reigns supreme. In an interview with PC Gamer, Diablo game director Brent Gibson said there were no plans for additional Diablo 4 expansions, as the team is instead "focused on seasons [for Diablo 4] and getting to Diablo 5." He added that Blizzard told the "story of Hatred" culminating in the Lord of Hatred expansion, and now it's moving forward to tell the "story of Terror." That doesn't mean support for Diablo 4 will end anytime soon. It sounds like Diablo 4's seasons will lead into the events of Diablo 5, even though the latter takes place a century later. That gives Blizzard room to set up Diablo 5's story, though Gibson said Blizzard doesn't "have a perfect picture" where it will all go because it wants to see how fans "react season to season." Diablo 4 is the only Diablo game to have received more than one expansion. Prior to release, Blizzard said it would receive "annual" expansions, though that quickly didn't come to pass. The game's Lord of Hatred expansion was released in April of this year, around a year-and-a-half after Diablo 4's first expansion, Vessel of Hatred. It's not a new expansion, but Diablo 4 is receiving a new class. The Amazon will join Diablo 4 as a standalone DLC next year. Diablo 4 Season 15, Hell's Legacy, begins September 15, and will see the return of iconic locations, items, Deckard Cain. The iconic Hordadrim will task players with battling memories of the Prime Evils from previous Diablo games, including Diablo himself.

title: Diablo 5’s Revealed Classes Are Throwbacks To Diablo 3, With One Exception
description: Diablo 5 isn't coming until Spring 2029, but Blizzard has already revealed three of the game's playable classes. Two of them will be familiar to Diablo 3 fans: the Monk and Demon Hunter. The third will be an all-new class, the Plague Knight. The Plague Knight sounds similar to Death Knights from Blizzard's other fantasy franchise and are described as "walking death" that spread disease and pestilence wherever they go, then consume it to increase their power. Blizzard revealed plenty of new details about Diablo 5 during a panel and subsequent blog post following the game's cinematic reveal as part of the BlizzCon 2026 opening ceremony. In addition to the three classes, Blizzard outlined the state of Sanctuary in Diablo 5 and how players will navigate it. Rather than journeying to towns, players will instead build a wandering caravan of survivors in a world that's been destroyed, and currently ruled, by Diablo himself. According to a developer blog post, Diablo 5's world will be "procedural," where terrain, monsters, and points of interest will change in the wake of the Lord of Terror's influence. As for the survivors that players will call allies, Blizzard said they will serve roles as vendors and companions. Two examples of companions that will accompany players are a former Sister of the Sightless Eye and a lost treasure goblin searching for meaning "in a world where greed has lost its meaning," Blizzard said. Though Diablo 5 is still early in development, there was some information about how it will play compared to Diablo 4. An early look at the game's inventory screen and items is extremely reminiscent of Diablo 2. Blizzard said it's a goal for items in Diablo 5 to be "readable, memorable, and worth chasing across hundreds of hours." Like in Diablo 2, items will take up more space in one's inventory depending on their size. Blizzard also confirmed item sets will return, as will Diablo 2-style runes and runewords. Blizzard may be putting the focus on Diablo 5,…
